_about: Evergreen material for The People's Watch monthly newsletter. Every factual item carries its source and was taken from the book's verified-facts table. Add items freely; keep each one short, plain and checkable.

1.title: When paper became as good as gold
1.text: On January 1, 1879, the greenbacks printed to fight the Civil War became redeemable in gold at full value again, under the Resumption Act of 1875. It took fourteen years to get there, and the amount of greenbacks had been fixed by law the year before at $346,681,016.

2.title: The month Lincoln's government printed money
2.text: On February 25, 1862, President Lincoln signed the Legal Tender Act, creating the 'greenbacks': paper money issued by the Treasury, not borrowed from anyone. Exactly one year later, on February 25, 1863, he signed the National Currency Act, which went the other way: bank notes backed by federal bonds. America ran both experiments at once.
2.source: Legal Tender Act (Feb 25, 1862); National Currency Act (Feb 25, 1863); OCC history

3.title: The Chicago Plan
3.text: In March 1933, in the depths of the Depression, a group of University of Chicago economists mailed a memo to about forty people proposing that banks hold full reserves against checking deposits, so a run could never take down the money people pay with. It went nowhere then. The book borrows its core idea.

4.title: A 23-year-old printer makes the case for paper money
4.text: On April 3, 1729, Benjamin Franklin, then 23, published 'A Modest Enquiry into the Nature and Necessity of a Paper-Currency.' Two years later he won the job of printing Pennsylvania's money, which he called 'a very profitable Jobb.' Decades later he credited two things for the paper's steady value: legal-tender status and keeping the quantity within bounds.
4.source: Founders Online, Franklin Papers; Franklin, Feb 13, 1767

5.title: 'Not worth a Continental'
5.text: The Continental dollar, printed to pay for the Revolution, was issued in eleven batches from 1775 to 1779 and stopped circulating as money after May 1781. Too many were printed with no limit, the classic warning about money without a rule. Historians still argue about how much of the collapse that explains.

6.title: The country that voted on its money
6.text: On June 10, 2018, Swiss voters decided whether only their central bank should create money, a plan much like this book's. It lost, 24.3% yes to 75.7% no. In the post-vote survey, the top reason no-voters gave was risk and uncertainty about an untested system. That is exactly why The People's Watch tests in public first.
6.source: Swiss federal results; VOTO post-vote study (July 2018)

7.title: The bank the world tried to close
7.text: In July 1944, the delegates at Bretton Woods passed Resolution V, recommending that the Bank for International Settlements, the central bankers' bank in Basel, be liquidated 'at the earliest possible moment.' It never was. Today 63 central banks own it.
7.source: Bretton Woods Resolution V (July 1944); BIS Annual Report

8.title: The day the dollar left gold
8.text: On August 15, 1971, President Nixon closed the 'gold window,' ending foreign governments' right to swap dollars for gold. From that day, the dollar's value has rested on how much of it is created and on trust, which is why the rule for creating it matters so much.

9.title: An empty chair for 64 years
9.text: The Federal Reserve chair had a seat on the board of the Bank for International Settlements from the start, but the Fed did not take it until September 13, 1994. For 64 years the American chair sat empty, because earlier Fed boards worried about entanglement in a European bankers' club.

10.title: The experiment that taught everyone a lesson
10.text: In October 1979, the Federal Reserve began targeting the amount of money instead of interest rates. By late 1982 it had pulled back, because the link between the money stock and spending kept shifting. That is why the book's rule watches actual prices, not just the money supply.
10.source: Federal Reserve History; St. Louis Fed

11.title: The secret meeting that was real
11.text: In November 1910, a handful of the most powerful bankers in America slipped away to a private club on Jekyll Island, Georgia, traveling under first names only, to draft a banking plan. One of them, Frank Vanderlip, later admitted he had been 'as secretive, indeed, as furtive as any conspirator.' What they drafted became the blueprint for the Federal Reserve.
11.source: Vanderlip, From Farm Boy to Financier (1935)

12.title: Two days before Christmas
12.text: On December 23, 1913, President Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act. The House had passed it 298 to 60, the Senate 43 to 25. Critics make much of the date, but the bill had been debated for months. A political settlement, as the book puts it, and settlements can be reopened.

myths.claim: The Fed has never been audited.
myths.text: The twelve Reserve Banks are audited every year by an outside accounting firm, and the Government Accountability Office has had authority to audit the Fed since 1978. The real gap is narrower and more interesting: the GAO is barred from reviewing monetary-policy decisions themselves.

myths.claim: Since 2020, banks can lend unlimited money because reserve requirements are zero.
myths.text: Reserve requirements did drop to zero in March 2020. But what limits a bank's lending is its capital (its own cushion against losses) and finding borrowers who will pay it back. The honest critique is different: bank money rises and falls with lending, and nobody votes on it.
myths.source: Federal Reserve (March 15/26, 2020); The People's Money, Ch. 2

myths.claim: The Fed made $16 trillion in secret loans in 2008.
myths.text: The $16.1 trillion figure counts every loan each time it was rolled over: a $10 billion overnight loan renewed 100 times shows up as $1 trillion. The most outstanding at any one time was a little over $1 trillion. Still enormous, and the details were kept from the public until Congress and a lawsuit forced them out.

myths.claim: Woodrow Wilson said, 'I have unwittingly ruined my country.'
myths.text: This quote is everywhere online, but there is no record of Wilson saying it. Repeating it hands defenders of the current system an easy way to dismiss everything else. The accurate history is strong enough on its own.

myths.claim: Minutes from Jekyll Island show the bankers agreed to avoid the words 'central bank.'
myths.text: No minutes of the 1910 Jekyll Island meeting exist; that quotation was made up and repeated until it sounded like history. The real admission is better: one attendee wrote that he had been 'as secretive, indeed, as furtive as any conspirator.'

myths.claim: The banks own the Fed and pocket its profits.
myths.text: Member banks must hold Reserve Bank stock and they elect most Reserve Bank directors. That part is real. But the dividend is capped by law, and profits above it go to the Treasury. In 2022, dividends were about $1.2 billion and remittances to the Treasury about $76 billion. The bigger payment to banks today is interest on their reserves.
myths.source: Federal Reserve releases; The People's Money, Ch. 2

myths.claim: Debt can never be repaid because the money to pay the interest was never created.
myths.text: Interest is paid out of income that keeps circulating, not out of a fixed pile of money, so this argument does not hold. The real concern does not need it: debt has grown faster than the income that services it for decades, and interest now takes about 19.5 cents of every federal revenue dollar.
myths.source: The People's Money, Ch. 1 and 4; Treasury MTS (FY2026)

myths.claim: The Bank for International Settlements is immune from all laws and can't be audited.
myths.text: The BIS has treaty immunities like other international organizations, with written exceptions, and it is audited every year by an outside firm. The fair concern is accountability: its most important meetings are private, with no published minutes.
myths.source: BIS Headquarters Agreement (1987); BIS Annual Report

explainers.title: What's a 'log point'?
explainers.text: It's a way of measuring change that adds up neatly. For small changes, a log point is almost exactly a percent: prices 0.5 log points above target are about 0.5% above. We use it because it makes the math come out the same whether prices go up then down or down then up.

explainers.title: Why aim for zero inflation instead of 2%?
explainers.text: Picture a carpenter whose tape measure shrinks a little every year. At 2% inflation, prices double in about 35 years, so a dollar saved at the start of a career buys half as much at the end. The book's rule aims for a tape measure that holds its length. Whether money can be made to behave that way is exactly what's being tested.

explainers.title: What is 'the brake'?
explainers.text: If prices run more than 3% above target for two quarters in a row, the Treasury must offer Stabilization Bills: short-term savings bonds that pay interest. Money used to buy them is parked, like cars in a garage, and can't be spent until the bills mature. Nobody's balance is ever cut; people choose to buy.

explainers.title: What's a digital fingerprint?
explainers.text: Every file the system downloads gets a fingerprint (a 'hash'): a short code that changes completely if even one digit in the file changes. It works like a wax seal on an old letter. If the seal doesn't match, someone opened it.

explainers.title: What's the 'Eurodollar' system?
explainers.text: Banks in London, Tokyo and elsewhere can make loans in dollars and create dollar deposits, the same way an Ohio bank does, outside U.S. rules. By one Bank for International Settlements estimate, foreign institutions owed about $65 trillion in off-balance-sheet dollar promises in 2022. When they suddenly need dollars, the squeeze can come home.

explainers.title: Why three calculators?
explainers.text: Imagine three accountants adding up the same receipts, separately, in different rooms. If all three get the same total, you can trust it. If one disagrees, you stop and find out why before anyone spends a dime. The system does exactly that, every quarter.

explainers.title: What's SOFR, and why watch it?
explainers.text: SOFR is what it costs to borrow cash overnight using U.S. Treasury bonds as collateral, a bit like a pawn shop's rate when you hand over the safest possible watch. When it jumps above the rate the Fed pays banks on their reserves, cash is getting scarce in the plumbing of the financial system.

explainers.title: What does 'as published' data mean?
explainers.text: Government statistics get revised, like a newspaper printing corrections. The rule uses each number as it stood on the day of the calculation, the first edition, so a later revision can never quietly change a past result.

unknowns: Whether the rule would actually keep prices steady. What credit and mortgages would cost. Whether the switch could happen without serious disruption. Whether a cheaper reform could get most of the benefit. Those are the tests in Chapter 9, and we will report them, good or bad, as they come in.
